extracted.intended_audience: mathematics instructors, teachers, and students interested in mathematical pedagogy (college level)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for presenting, teaching, and discovering mathematics in classroom and textbook settings, including heuristics for problem solving, proof presentation, and fostering student discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of the Discovery Process
rubrics_metrics.description: The way to understanding is the way of the initial discovery — showing how something was originally thought out can aid classroom presentation, but the initial discovery may also be obscure or unnecessarily difficult and therefore not always the best presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t assume the historical discovery path is always best; sometimes reconstruct the discovery (or a variant) so students confront difficulties and breakthroughs. Example: author reconstructed a proof 'along slightly different (or even novel) lines' to avoid the traumatic step in the original proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build preliminary intuition before formal proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Before giving the formal proof, build intuition via simple lemmas, clear examples, and corollaries that set limits and show why the statement is plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elementary observations (e.g., 'The area of a circle is bisected by any diameter' and its converse) and corollaries (limits of generalization such as two- vs three-circle bisector results) to increase appreciation and understanding prior to formal derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parameterized/continuity arguments to demonstrate existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a parameterized function (e.g., p(θ) = percentage on one side as diameter rotates) and use continuity/orientation arguments (p(0)+p(180)=100%) to deduce existence of an intermediate value (e.g., a bisector).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model problems by letting an orientation vary over a full range and use continuity or parity/orientation symmetries to obtain intermediate values; the pancake-circle bisection example illustrates this strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalize stepwise from simple to general case
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove the statement first in a special or simpler setting (circle vs pancake), then remove simplifying assumptions to handle the general case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example progression: circle → circle + pancake → two general pancakes. This clarifies essential structure and avoids introducing overwhelming generality too soon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide alternative proofs that avoid traumatic steps
rubrics_metrics.description: If a standard proof contains a step that creates student resistance or confusion, construct a different proof that preserves necessary ideas but presents them in a less traumatic guise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author’s experience: after a crisis in class, he wrote and presented a 'slightly different proof which avoided the traumatic step' and found it more effective for student understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose limits and boundaries of generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out when a theorem does or does not generalize (e.g., two-circle problem has unique solution unless centers coincide; three-circle problem generally has no solution unless centers collinear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly discuss corollaries that set limits; knowledge of such limits increases appreciation of the original statement and prevents overgeneralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purely 'backward' textbook-style presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbook/monograph presentations often eliminate the discovery process, rearranging and polishing content according to logico-deductive canons; this brevity can obscure understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever possible, supplement polished presentations with the discovery context or reconstructed heuristics so students can see how ideas were found, not merely how they are best stated concisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid authoritarian or dogmatic lecturing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical instruction should invite reasoning together ('Come, let us reason together') rather than 'I tell you this is the way it is' (proof by coercion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware causes of dogmatism (time pressure, desire to appear brilliant, teacher ignorance or lack of confidence). Encourage exploratory, non-coercive classroom culture and give teachers space to 'fiddle around' pedagogically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and address student resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Students may show impatience, expect instant understanding, or resist material that requires prolonged struggle; better students may be particularly demanding of immediate comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach strategies for productive struggle: normalize that understanding takes time, build experience and heuristic strategies, encourage 'fiddling around', and help students accept that insight may require effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster the conditions for 'flash of insight' and teachable creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Creativity ('aha' moments) symbolizes a genuinely new understanding; while not democratic, creativity can be increased or decreased and—within limits—taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn by example and precept from masters; transmit strategies and heuristics that increase probability of insight. Provide opportunities and exercises aimed at discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya's Four-step Problem Solving Framework
rubrics_metrics.description: How to Solve It — First: understand the problem. Second: find the connection between data and unknown (construct a plan). Third: carry out your plan. Fourth: examine the solution obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this global plan as a scaffold for student problem solving and classroom organization; follow with 'molecular' heuristics when students are stuck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya's molecular heuristics (problem-solving moves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete tactics to call on when solving problems: e.g., if you cannot solve, look for related problems; work backwards; work forwards; narrow or widen conditions; seek counterexamples; guess and test; divide and conquer; change conceptual mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these heuristics flexibly and teach students to recognize which move may be appropriate at a given stage; amplify each with examples and exercises as Polya does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis heuristics (Schoenfeld): draw diagram and examine special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Key analysis moves: 1) DRAW A DIAGRAM if at all possible. 2) EXAMINE SPECIAL CASES: choose special values, examine limiting cases, set integer parameters 1,2,3... to look for induction patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to concretize abstract problems visually and test tractable special/limiting cases to develop intuition and spot structures or counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify the problem: exploit symmetry and WLOG (without loss of generality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to simplify by exploiting symmetry or applying 'without loss of generality' arguments (including scaling) to reduce complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach reduction techniques that preserve essential difficulty while making the problem more tractable; show how WLOG assumptions can clarify rather than hide subtleties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration heuristics (Schoenfeld): equivalent and modified problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploratory tactics: consider essentially equivalent problems (replace conditions by equivalents, recombine elements, introduce auxiliaries, reformulate viewpoints), slightly modified problems (choose subgoals, relax conditions, decompose domain), and broadly modified problems (construct analogous problems with fewer variables, hold variables fixed, exploit related problems' form/givens/conclusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stuck, reformulate the problem in nearby variants to gain insight; exploit both result and method from easier related problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifying your solution: specific and general tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests to validate a solution: Specific tests — uses all pertinent data, conforms to reasonable estimates, withstands symmetry/dimension/scale checks. General tests — can it be obtained differently, substantiated by special cases, reduced to known results, or used to generate known results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to apply these checks as a routine verification stage (Polya/Schoenfeld guidance); incorporate such verification into grading and feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal clues gradually to enable discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: When reconstructing a proof for pedagogical purposes, reveal one clue at a time, slowly, so that readers or students may experience a small discovery themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polya-style classroom storytelling: give successive hints and build the figure or notation gradually so students can 'seize the main idea' rather than be overwhelmed by a finished argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lakatosian proofs-and-refutations heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an iterative model: present a conjecture/seed, expect and examine counterexamples, modify the statement and proof, produce new counterexamples, and refine again — modeling mathematical knowledge development as fallible and corrigible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply in class by using open-ended problems where student counterexamples lead to reformulation; fosters ownership and deeper understanding but requires careful facilitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seed selection and 'watering the seed' classroom method
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a simple, interesting 'seed' conjecture and have students 'water' it — test examples, provide counterexamples, propose refinements — so the conjecture grows into a well-formulated theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select seeds of appropriate difficulty and interest; allow the class to engage in cycles of conjecture, testing, refutation, and reformulation (example: 'magic numbers' exploration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to drive reformulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat local and global counterexamples as essential data that force refinement of definitions and theorems (e.g., single-digit vs multi-digit reinterpretation in 'magic numbers').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to propose counterexamples and to analyze whether they invalidate the claim, indicate a need for additional hypotheses, or suggest a fruitful generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage reformulation and precise definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When naive conjectures fail, adjust definitions (narrow or widen) or domain (allow N to be groups of digits) to clarify the intended question and enable rigorous theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classroom episodes to illustrate how formal definitions evolve from informal observations; emphasize that careful specification of hypotheses is part of mathematical discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor aesthetic proofs that reveal the 'heart' of the matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic value in proofs is often associated with brevity and revealing the core reason (Proof II in √2 example), whereas longer contradiction-based proofs may feel plodding though formally valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss multiple proofs and explicitly compare their explanatory power; help students appreciate why some proofs are seen as more enlightening and how that influences mathematical taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize conscious vs unconscious mathematizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate 'unconscious mathematics' (automatic, inherent in nature and behaviour) from 'conscious mathematics' (learned, symbolic, brain-mediated reasoning); both play roles in problem solving and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge non-symbolic problem-solving abilities (number sense, space sense, kinesthetic sense) in teaching and build on them when appropriate; reflection can often reveal hybrid strategies students use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and employ analog-experimental and analytic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscious mathematics can be 'analog-experimental' (intuitive, spatial, quick, possibly non-symbolic) or 'analytic' (symbolic, formal). Both are valuable and sometimes complementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analog approaches for intuition and initial exploration, and analytic approaches for formalization and proof. Teach students to move between modes ('change the conceptual mode') as Polya recommends.
